people.name: John McFadden
people.notes: From Carrowmore, Co. Mayo; long duo with piper James Early; 'John McFadden's Favourite' bears his name; on the O'Neill wax cylinders (c.1904).

people.name: Sgt. James Early
people.role: piper, flute and fiddle player, reed-maker
people.notes: Source of 'Sergeant Early's Dream'; hosted visiting musicians including Turlough McSweeney in 1893.

people.name: Bernard 'Barney' Delaney
people.notes: From Tullamore; O'Neill's brother-in-law; source of 'The Slashing Reel' and 'The Milliner's Daughter'; O'Neill once wrote to Havana police asking them to find him.

people.name: Edward Cronin
people.notes: From Limerick Junction; composed 'Rogers O'Neill', 'Caroline O'Neill's Hornpipe', 'Doctor O'Neill' and the 'Bantry Hornpipe' for the Chief's family.

people.name: John Ennis
people.role: piper and flute player, Irish Music Club president/secretary
people.notes: From Co. Kildare; source of 'The Gold Ring' and 'Kildare Fancy'. His son Tom Ennis, a Chicago-born piper who later recorded in New York, is remembered in the jig 'Young Tom Ennis'.

people.name: Selena O'Neill
people.notes: Trained at the Chicago Musical College; arranged O'Neill's later books (1910-1924) and a 1940 edition of the Dance Music.

people.name: Patrick Stack and Edward Mullaney
people.notes: Made the 1926 recording of 'The Chicago Reel'. Mullaney was Joe Shannon's uncle and first pipes teacher.

people.name: Pat Roche
people.role: step dancer, céilí band leader, dance teacher
people.notes: Led the Harp & Shamrock Orchestra at the 1934 World's Fair Irish Village (Decca recordings); interviewed for the 1977 Chicago Ethnic Arts Project.

people.name: Johnny McGreevy
people.notes: Recorded with Pat Roche (1934) and pianist Eleanor Kane (1935); LP 'McGreevy and Cooley' (about 1974) with flute player Seamus Cooley; composed the reel 'McGreevy's'; a major influence on Liz Carroll.

people.name: Eleanor (Kane) Neary
people.notes: Recorded for Decca in 1935; the jig and hornpipe 'Eleanor Neary's' are named for her (the jig is also called 'The Chicago').

people.name: Terry 'Cuz' Teahan
people.notes: Kerry-born Chicago musician recorded for the 1977 Chicago Ethnic Arts Project; composed the jig 'Gaelic Park'; polkas bear his name.

people.name: Kevin Henry
people.notes: From Co. Mayo; helped set up what became the Irish Musicians Association of America; knew O'Neill's secretary Teresa Geary.

people.name: Noel Rice
people.notes: From Co. Offaly; led north-side learning sessions in the 1970s that brought in a young Seán Cleland.

people.name: Jimmy Keane
people.notes: Five All-Ireland titles; 1975 senior duet champion with Liz Carroll; later in Bohola with Seán Cleland.

people.name: Seán Cleland
people.role: fiddler, founder of the Irish Music School of Chicago (2003)
people.notes: Led a Wednesday session at Mrs. Murphy & Sons Irish Bistro (documented in the Digital Chicago exhibit; current status for another thread to check).

people.name: Tommy Dandurand
people.role: fiddler, National Barn Dance house band leader
people.notes: Retired Kankakee streetcar operator; 14 Gennett sides in 1927 with caller Ed Goodreau.

people.name: Frank Hart and William McCormick
people.notes: From Aurora and Marseilles, IL; placed in WLS's 1924 fiddle contest and became the image of the early Barn Dance.

people.name: Win Stracke
people.notes: Blacklisted TV performer ('Chicago Two' with Studs Terkel); People's Songs board member.

people.name: Frank Hamilton
people.role: multi-instrumentalist, Old Town School co-founder and teacher
people.notes: Brought Bess Lomax Hawes's group-teaching method and invented the 'Second Half' sing; joined the Weavers in 1962.

people.name: Dawn Greening
people.notes: Hosted the first $2 guitar classes in her Oak Park home; housed Odetta, Peggy Seeger, Joan Baez and Ramblin' Jack Elliott.

people.name: Big Bill Broonzy
people.notes: Great Migration arrival in the early 1920s; part of 'I Come for to Sing'; played at the OTS opening night.

people.name: Studs Terkel
people.notes: WFMT host whose 5,000+ conversations form the WFMT Studs Terkel Radio Archive.

people.name: Bob Gibson
people.notes: Brought Frank Hamilton and Joan Baez to Chicago stages.

people.name: Albert Grossman
people.notes: Opened the Gate of Horn; later co-founded Newport and managed Dylan.

people.name: George and Gerry Armstrong
people.notes: George's bagpipes opened OTS's first night; the couple made field trips to record fading traditions.

people.name: Earl Pionke
people.notes: Ran the Earl of Old Town 1962-1984; co-opened Somebody Else's Troubles in 1974.

people.name: Fred Holstein
people.notes: Resident at the Earl (from 1966) and Somebody Else's Troubles; co-owned Holstein's (closed 1987); mentored Steve Goodman. Brother Ed Holstein also performed and co-owned.

people.name: Steve Goodman
people.notes: Wrote 'City of New Orleans' (about an Illinois Central train) and 'Go Cubs Go'.

people.name: John Prine
people.notes: Launched at the Fifth Peg in 1969; Earl regular.

people.name: Bonnie Koloc
people.notes: Third member of the 'trinity of the Chicago folk scene'; Earl of Old Town fixture.

people.name: Bruce Kaplan
people.notes: Former UChicago Folklore Society president; founded Flying Fish Records in 1974; Liz Carroll recorded for the label.

people.name: Mary Wood Hinman
people.notes: Hull House teacher from about 1898; Hinman School (1904/05); taught Doris Humphrey; worked with John Dewey's school.

people.name: Lynn 'Chirps' Smith
people.notes: Learned from downstate Illinois old-timers (Harvey 'Pappy' Taylor, Noah Beavers); lead fiddle in the Volo Bogtrotters from 1985; later the New Bad Habits.

people.name: Paul Tyler (DrDosido)
people.notes: Historian of the National Barn Dance (Hayloft Gang book and film); Volo Bogtrotters from 1993; OTS teacher; runs fiddle workshops at Chicago pubs and Seman Violins.

people.name: Fred Campeau and Steve Rosen
people.notes: Volo Bogtrotters core members and fixtures of the Chicago old-time scene.

people.name: Mary Allsopp
people.notes: Glen Ellyn; Swedish/Norwegian fiddle club; informal 'Scandijams' in Wheeling 2013-2022.

people.name: Juel Ulven
people.notes: Inducted posthumously into the Fox Valley Arts Hall of Fame, 2026.

people.name: Nancy Buckalew
people.notes: Alabama-born; recorded at Johnny's Tavern, Cicero; played with Chicago musician Tennessee Slim; repertoire included 'Arkansas Traveler' and 'Bile Them Cabbage Down'.

people.name: Ted Johnson
people.role: second Old Town School teacher (1957 onward); co-founder of the Chicago Sacred Harp Singers; Sacred Harp composer
people.tradition: folk guitar, banjo, yodeling; Sacred Harp
people.notes: Died Oct 10, 2026 at 98. Taught at the school for more than 40 years and was later an Irish-fiddle student there; his tune 'New Agatite' is in the 1991 Sacred Harp; co-chaired the Midwest Convention with his wife Marcia; a memorial is planned at the school in January 2027.

people.name: Marcia Johnson
people.role: Sacred Harp organizer and folk singer
people.notes: Met Ted at the Old Town School in 1963; with Judy Hauff she took Hugh McGraw's 1985 call that led to the first Illinois State Convention.

people.name: Judy Hauff
people.role: Chicago Sacred Harp pioneer and composer; 1970s Old Town School regular
people.notes: Went to Holly Springs, GA after the 1985 Paxton convention; her memories of the 1970s all-night parties are in the school's history.

people.name: Ray Tate
people.role: Old Town School dean of faculty, then executive director 1969-1982
people.notes: Co-opened The Fifth Peg, where John Prine began in 1969.

people.name: Jim Hirsch
people.role: Old Town School executive director 1982-2000; led the turnaround and the 1998 move to Lincoln Square

people.name: Michael Miles
people.role: Old Town School program director from 1984; banjoist; rebuilt the curriculum
people.notes: Added fiddle, voice, percussion and early-childhood classes; started the La Peña Wednesday concert series in 1995.

people.name: Paul Tyler
people.role: Old Town School old-time ensemble teacher (with Steve Rosen, since 1990)

people.name: Mark Dvorak
people.role: long-time Old Town School folk guitar and banjo teacher; co-founder of the Plank Road String Band
people.notes: Woodstock Folk Festival Lifetime Achievement Award 2008.

people.name: Troy Anderson
people.role: Executive Director and CEO, Old Town School of Folk Music

people.name: Fleming Brown
people.role: early Old Town School banjo teacher
people.notes: Learned from WLS radio's Doc Hopkins; recorded Hobart Smith in 1963.

people.name: Rich Warren
people.role: WFMT Midnight Special producer from 1974, co-host from 1983, sole host 1996-2020
people.notes: Co-hosted the Woodstock Folk Festival from 2009.

people.name: Marilyn Rea Beyer
people.role: host of WFMT's The Midnight Special and Folkstage
people.notes: Folk Alliance International Folk DJ Hall of Fame 2023.

people.name: George Mattson
people.role: leader of the Plank Road sing-arounds (since the mid-1990s) and song circle (since 2011); former Old Town School guitar teacher

people.name: Tom and Chris Kastle
people.role: maritime singers; organizers of the Chicago Maritime Festival

people.name: Lee Murdock
people.notes: Woodstock Folk Festival Lifetime Achievement Award 2011 (with Joann Murdock); maritime Christmas concert at the Chicago Maritime Museum.

people.name: Amy Beth and Melodee Ladd
people.role: founders of the Woodstock Folk Festival (1986)
people.notes: Amy Beth received the festival's Lifetime Achievement Award in 2005.

people.name: John Williams
people.notes: Leads sessions at Galway Arms, the Celtic Knot and Clancy's.

people.name: Pauline Conneely
people.notes: Leads Chief O'Neill's Sunday and Harp and Fiddle Thursday; Carl Hession composed the reel "The Chicago Conneely" for her.

people.name: Larry Nugent & Frank Quinn
people.notes: Long-running Mrs. Murphy's session.

people.name: Sean Cleland
people.role: fiddle; Irish Music School of Chicago
people.notes: Led Chief O'Neill's sessions (2000s-2010s) and the 2011 IAHC Thursday session; runs the Sunday family session.

people.name: James (Jim) Conway & Mike Austin
people.role: session leaders; Old Town School teachers
people.notes: Fifth Province Thursday session; Conway learned from Offaly flute player Noel Rice.

people.name: Eleanor Kane Neary & Jimmy Neary
people.notes: Encouraged the young Chicago players of the 1960s-70s; Liz Carroll learned the jig "Eleanor Neary's" from Eleanor.

people.name: Kell & Mike Chole
people.notes: Clancy's Sunday and Wednesday sessions.

people.name: Brendan Houlihan
people.notes: Tuesday set dancing at Gaelic Park.

people.name: Dan Cahill & Alan Beale
people.notes: Francis O'Neill Club; Alan Beale Workshop Weekend.

people.name: Eric Zorn
people.role: contra caller; fiddle & guitar with the Ladies Banjo Society of Illinois
people.notes: Former Chicago Tribune columnist; calls at CBDC and plays alongside his son Ben Zorn.

people.name: Georges Augustin
people.notes: Organiser of the Monday dance.

people.name: Meg Dedolph
people.notes: Most-booked caller on the CBDC calendar (14 in-MSA dates Nov 2025-Oct 2026): FVFS, Plank Road, Ridgeville, Les Rats Mouillés.

people.name: Moose Flores
people.notes: Second most-booked caller in the past year.

people.name: Andrea Craft
people.notes: Spokesperson for gender-free terminology (2019).

people.name: Mady Newfield
people.tradition: English country / international folk dance / Scottish
people.notes: Founded Fermilab International Folk Dancing (1988) and directed it for 32 years; co-founded Chicagoland ECD (2006); directs June Camp; teaches for RSCDS Chicago.

people.name: Tammy Ravitts Bretscher
people.notes: Co-founder of Chicagoland ECD; Jane Austen scholar (JASNA).

people.name: Cheryl Yenter
people.notes: Chicagoland North (Glenview).

people.name: Paul Tyler ("Dr. Dosido")
people.notes: Founded the Fiddle Club of the World (Chicago Chapter, 2008) and the Midwest Fiddle Championship (2003); taught "Ethnic Music in Chicago Neighborhoods"; now runs the Dunelands chapter in Miller Beach, IN.

people.name: Steve Haberichter
people.notes: Hosts the Hailstorm Wednesday jam.

people.name: Aaron Smith
people.notes: Hosts Bluegrass Breakdown; has played bass with the Ladies Banjo Society.

people.name: Paul Collins
people.notes: Turned his square dance group into the Chicago Morris Dancers (1969). A Paul Collins now posts on Ethnic Dance Chicago's Virtual Dance Room; that this is the same person is likely but unverified.

people.name: Edie Spear
people.notes: Taught at June Camp and Oconomowoc camp; danced on Zoom into her late 90s.

timeline.event: Lyon & Healy founded in Chicago as a sheet-music shop; by 1900 it is making harps, guitars, mandolins, banjos and ukuleles.
Francis O'Neill (b. 1848, Tralibane, Co. Cork) settles in Chicago after years at sea; he joins the police in 1873 (sources differ on the arrival year).
Piper/fiddler James Early (Cloone, Co. Leitrim) moves to Chicago and joins the police; his house becomes a hub for visiting musicians.
Washburn brand of fretted instruments established in Chicago.
Hull House settlement opens on the Near West Side; around 1898 Mary Wood Hinman begins teaching immigrant folk dances there.
Harmony Company founded; it later becomes the largest US instrument maker (about 10 million guitars, 1945-1975).
World's Columbian Exposition: pipers Patsy Touhey and Turlough McSweeney play in the fair's Irish villages; McSweeney lodges with James Early from May to October.
Mary Wood Hinman joins the Hull House dance faculty; settlement classes teach immigrants' children folk dances.

O'Neill becomes Chicago's Chief of Police (1901-1905); the Irish Music Club of Chicago forms around this time, the earliest known organization of Irish traditional musicians in North America (fl. c.1901-09).
Chicago police chief Francis O'Neill publishes O'Neill's Music of Ireland, compiled largely from immigrant musicians in Chicago.
O'Neill's Music of Ireland (1,850 tunes) published in Chicago, transcribed largely by fiddler Sgt. James O'Neill.
Police chief Francis O'Neill publishes O'Neill's Music of Ireland, largely gathered from Chicago players.
Mary Wood Hinman opens her School of Gymnastic and Folk Dance in Hyde Park (some sources say 1905), training women to teach folk dance in schools, parks and settlements.
Hinman School of Gymnastic and Folk Dance founded in Hyde Park.
The Dance Music of Ireland ('O'Neill's 1001') published; it remains the core printed source of Irish dance tunes.
University High School boys dance the morris "Bean Setting" at Bartlett Gym, UChicago.
O'Neill publishes Irish Minstrels and Musicians, with biographies of his Chicago sources and the Irish Music Club photograph (p. 479).
Thomas A. Dorsey moves to Chicago; gospel later grows from Bronzeville churches.

April 19: WLS's Barn Dance (later National Barn Dance) debuts; announcer George D. Hay leaves after about 18 months to start what became the Grand Ole Opry. Kankakee streetcar man Tommy Dandurand leads the house fiddlers from fall 1924.
Future NEA Fellow and uilleann piper Joe Shannon's family emigrates from Mayo to Chicago.
Chicago fiddler Patrick Stack and piper Edward Mullaney record 'The Chicago Reel'; Tom Owen's WLS Barn Dance Trio records 'Hell on the Wabash' for Gennett.
Kenneth Warren opens his violin business in the Loop.
Tommy Dandurand & His Barn Dance Fiddlers (with Rube Tronson and caller Ed Goodreau) cut 14 sides for Gennett.
Polish Highlanders Alliance of North America (ZPPA) founded; 90th anniversary in 2019.
National Barn Dance moves to the Eighth Street Theatre, where it charges admission (said to be the only radio show that did). O'Neill donates his library to the University of Notre Dame.
Thomas A. Dorsey, the 'father of gospel music', is based at Pilgrim Baptist Church, making Chicago the cradle of the gospel-chorus movement.
Thomas A. Dorsey co-founds the National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses in Chicago.
Century of Progress fair: piper Joe Shannon, aged about 14, plays in the Irish Village with dancer Pat Roche's céilí band; Roche's Harp & Shamrock Orchestra records for Decca.
Century of Progress fair's "Merrie England" village features morris and sword dancers.
Adam Popovich becomes director of the Sloboda choir at St. Archangel Michael Serbian Orthodox Church; the Popovich Brothers tamburitza orchestra is a fixture of Chicago and Indiana steel towns.
Francis O'Neill dies in Chicago (January 26).
October 25: Alan Lomax records 'Mrs. Hulan' singing with a kantele (Finnish zither) in Chicago during his Great Lakes field trip.
Win Stracke, Studs Terkel, Big Bill Broonzy and Larry Lane begin the revue 'I Come for to Sing', an early college-circuit folk show.
Win Stracke, Studs Terkel, Larry Lane and Big Bill Broonzy start the 'I Come For to Sing' folk revue, an early college-campus folk tour.
U of C Folk Dancers perform morris and hold contra dances at Ida Noyes Hall.
American Indian Center of Chicago founded (first urban Indian center in the US) amid federal Relocation; Lithuanian ensemble Grandis founded the same year.
WFMT starts 'The Midnight Special' (first host Mike Nichols), broadcasting Chicago's folk community.
Mike Nichols starts WFMT's The Midnight Special, a Saturday folk program that is still on air.
First Chicago Powwow, inferred from the 73rd annual in 2026.

Albert Grossman and Les Brown open the Gate of Horn (755 N. Dearborn), probably the first US nightclub devoted to folk music. In the same decade flute player Kevin Henry and others found what became the Irish Musicians Association of America (year from secondary summary).
Irish Musicians Association of America founded (19 Aug) at the Midland Hotel; later a Comhaltas branch.
Old Town School of Folk Music opens at 333 W. North Ave (Nov 29 or Dec 1), founded by Win Stracke, Frank Hamilton and Dawn Greening; 160 students by Feb 1958.
Old Town School of Folk Music founded.
Milan Opacich joins the Gary Fire Department and builds tamburitzas in the firehouse basement.
Delmark Records moves from St. Louis to Chicago; the Old Town School already has 160 enrolled students plus 200 at informal sings.
Polka 'moonlight dances' in Chicago draw thousands; the first national polka convention follows in 1963, leading to the International Polka Association's conventions.
First University of Chicago Folk Festival (Stanley Brothers, New Lost City Ramblers, Elizabeth Cotten, Roscoe Holcomb, Willie Dixon).
Earl Pionke opens the Earl of Old Town (1615 N. Wells); Frank Hamilton leaves the Old Town School to join the Weavers.
Frank Hamilton leaves to join the Weavers; Ray Tate becomes dean of faculty.
Council of the Southern Mountains opens the Chicago Southern Center in Uptown, 'Hillbilly Heaven' for Appalachian migrants.
With the Gate of Horn and other clubs closed, Earl Pionke's Earl of Old Town on Wells Street turns to folk and becomes the center of the scene until 1984.
Old Town School moves to 909 W. Armitage; the National Barn Dance leaves the air (WGN, after WLS dropped it in 1960).
Old Town School moves to the 1896 'Aldine' building at 909 W Armitage.
John Prine launches his career at the Fifth Peg; Steve Goodman, Prine and Bonnie Koloc define the 'Earl' era.
John Prine starts his career at The Fifth Peg, opened by Old Town School people including Ray Tate.
Chicago Morris Dancers formed from Paul Collins' square dance group.
Two Way Street Coffee House opens as a teen drop-in center at First Congregational Church, Downers Grove.
Segundo Ruiz Belvis Cultural Center founded, Chicago's longest-standing Latino cultural center.
Amazingrace coffeehouse opens at Northwestern (Evanston; 1971-1980); Dunwich releases 'Gathering at the Earl of Old Town'.
Chicago Irish Radio's Mike O'Connor Show goes on air (still live in 2026); Alligator Records founded.
Muntu Dance Theatre founded.
Comhaltas Ceoltóirí Éireann enters North America; the Mid-West region later includes Chicago branches.
Bruce Kaplan, former UChicago Folklore Society president, founds Flying Fish Records; Pionke, Goodman, Fred Holstein and partners open Somebody Else's Troubles (2470 N. Lincoln).
Bruce Kaplan founds Flying Fish Records.
Chicago Israeli Folk Dancing weekly session begins (March).
Ensemble Español (Libby Komaiko) and Natya Dance Theatre (Hema Rajagopalan) founded.
Chicago-born Liz Carroll, 18, wins the All-Ireland senior fiddle title, and the senior duet with Jimmy Keane; the folk quarterly 'Come for to Sing' launches.
Fox Valley Folklore Society's weekly Wednesday sing-around begins (still weekly in 2026); the 'Come for to Sing' folk journal launches; the Chicago School of Violin Making is founded.
Irish American Heritage Center founded; it buys the former Mayfair College building in 1985.

Library of Congress/Illinois Arts Council Chicago Ethnic Arts Project documents 26 communities (344 tapes, 14,000 photos), including the Midwest Fleadh at Bogan High School. The first Fox Valley Folk Festival is held.
First Fox Valley Folk Festival (year inferred from the 49th edition in 2025).
First Fox Valley Folk Festival in Geneva (derived from the 49th edition in 2025).
Downstate fiddler Lynn 'Chirps' Smith moves to Chicago and becomes a mainstay of Chicago Barn Dance Company dances.
First Taste of Polonia at the Copernicus Center (some accounts say 1980).
Hromovytsia Ukrainian Dance Ensemble founded.
FitzGerald family buys the Deer Lodge in Berwyn and opens FitzGerald's.
Scottish country dance class starts in Palos Park (7 Feb); RSCDS branch status in 1987.
Old Town School enrollment collapses to about 300 a week, nearly $60,000 in debt. FitzGerald's American Music Festival (Berwyn) and Milwaukee Irish Fest both begin.
Old Town School near collapse: enrollment down to about 300 a week from 1,000+, nearly $60,000 in the red; Ray Tate resigns in 1982 and Jim Hirsch takes over.
First NEA National Heritage Fellowships include Chicago-area tamburitza master Adam Popovich; Mexican Folkloric Dance Company of Chicago and Trinity Irish Dance founded.
Maxwell Street Klezmer Band founded; Joe Shannon named NEA Fellow.
Chicago Blues Festival begins; the górale Festiwal na Góralską Nutę starts around this year (inferred from numbering).
Earl of Old Town closes; Chicago Blues Festival begins; Volo Bogtrotters old-time band forms (to 2002). Steve Goodman dies.
Earl of Old Town closes (per the Old Town School's history; a blog says 1993); Michael Miles becomes program director.
Chicago Gospel Music Festival begins.
Chicago Gospel Music Festival begins; IAHC buys the Mayfair School; Gaelic Park opens in Oak Forest; OTS launches its Festival of Latin Music.

First Illinois State Sacred Harp Convention (Paxton, May 25), organized by Chicago and Charleston singers with Hugh McGraw; Plank Road Folk Music Society founded; Wiggleworms and the Festival of Latin Music start at the Old Town School.
Plank Road Folk Music Society founded in the western suburbs.
First Woodstock Folk Festival.
Renovated Old Town School reopens on Armitage with a Resource Center; Holstein's club closes; first Chicago Scots Highland Games.
Renovated 909 W Armitage reopens; the Old Town School's enrollment doubles between 1984 and 1987.
Michael Flatley and Sunnyland Slim named NEA Fellows.
Fermilab International Folk Dancing founded by Mady Newfield.
Lake County Folk Club founded; Front Porch Music opens in Valparaiso, IN.
Andrew Calhoun founds Waterbug Records (Glen Ellyn).
Pierogi Fest begins in Whiting, IN; Fiesta Boricua reportedly begins on Paseo Boricua.
Sones de México Ensemble founded in Pilsen; Klezmer Music Foundation and Junior Klezmer Orchestra begin; Liz Carroll named NEA Fellow; cimbalom player Nicolae Feraru moves to Chicago.
Bloodshot Records founded; the 'insurgent country' scene gathers at the Hideout (new owners 1996).
Celtic Fest Chicago begins in Grant Park (to 2010).
Eddie Blazonczyk (polka) and Pops Staples (gospel) named NEA Fellows.
Old Town School opens in the 1931 Hild Library, Lincoln Square (425-seat hall), with the first Folk & Roots Festival in Welles Park.
Old Town School opens its Lincoln Square home in the former Hild Library (425-430-seat hall); first Folk & Roots Festival in Welles Park; revenue nearly doubles between 1997 and 1999.
AfriCaribe founded by Evaristo 'Tito' Rodriguez.
Siumni Polish Highlander ensemble founded.
Fiddler Seán Cleland founds the Irish Music School of Chicago.
Irish Music School of Chicago founded by Seán Cleland; Chicago Maritime Festival begins in its present form.
Midwest Fiddle Championship begins at the Old Town School festival; Galway Arms and Quigley's sessions listed on The Session (2003-04).
Koko Taylor and tamburitza maker Milan Opacich named NEA Fellows.
Chicagoland English Country Dancers founded (January).
Jarochicanos son jarocho collective forms as a youth workshop.
Fiddle Club of the World (Chicago Chapter) convened by Paul Tyler.
La Escuelita Bombera de Corazón founded by Ivelisse Díaz.
Mariachi Matters free youth program starts in Romeoville.
Thursday session starts in the IAHC Fifth Province Pub (Sean Cleland), later led by Conway & Austin. ScandiJam at the Swedish American Museum also starts around this time.
Folk & Roots Festival moves onto Lincoln Avenue as Square Roots (per Anvara; other sources imply 2011).
Earl Pionke dies (April); Frankfort Bluegrass Festival begins (inferred).
Clancy's (Oak Lawn) becomes a south-suburban session hub, at one point with 3-4 sessions a week.
First Jarochicanos 'Huapango de Primavera' fandango (Apr 4).
Abbey Pub (opened 1973), the Northwest Side's Irish music hall, closes after a fire.
Los Pleneros de Don Segundo formed at SRBCC.
Queer Contra Chicago relaunches; organisers adopt role-free terms that later spread to the wider scene.
Ballet Folklórico de Chicago founded; it now reports 400+ students.
OTS board announces the sale of its Armitage campus (Oct 2018); protest follows and the building was still in use in 2025.
October: Old Town School board announces the sale of 909 W Armitage to build an endowment, provoking protests; Hey Nonny opens in Arlington Heights.
Old Town School teachers vote to unionize (IFT); first contract reached June 2022 after pandemic-era bargaining.
Executive director Bau Graves resigns (January); faculty vote to join the Illinois Federation of Teachers (Jan 16); the board drops the Armitage sale (March).
COVID: the Blues Festival is cancelled for the first time; OTS moves classes online (more than 65% of teachers and students continued, per its 2020 report).

COVID: Two Way Street moves online and sets a single-concert donation record; Rich Warren retires from The Midnight Special after 37 years as co-host or host and Marilyn Rea Beyer takes over; FitzGerald's sold days before the shutdown.
COVID-19: the Gaelic Park Thursday session lapses; the Chicago Folk Dance Council listing stops updating (2019); IFD moves partly to Zoom.
Bloodshot Records closes its office and is sold to Exceleration Music (October).
First Old Town School faculty union contract (June); Uncommon Ground's Edgewater location closes (October).
Post-COVID session wave: Jimmy Keane and Kavan Donohoe start Galway Bay (Tue) and Kerryman (Sun) sessions; Wolfhound Tuesday session listed.
Celtic Knot (Evanston) closes 30 April; Jimmy Keane revives the Gaelic Park session in September.
AIC holds its first Powwow at the Lake (Foster Beach, 500+); Bril Barrett named NEA Fellow; African Festival of the Arts takes a one-year hiatus.
Ella Jenkins, Chicago's 'first lady of children's music', dies at 100 (Nov 9).
First Evanston Folk Festival (Sep 7-8, about 5,000 a day).
McHenry County sessions start at the Stanchion Pub (Harvard) and Kishwaukee Brewing (Woodstock); CBDC Monday draws 93 dancers on 30 Dec.
AfriCaribe's 25th year; 72nd Chicago Powwow (host drum Smokeytown); African Festival of the Arts returns (35th); Logan Center starts a monthly blues jam.
Rebound: OTS reports 24,542 students, 200+ ticketed shows (63,235 tickets), 45,000 at Square Roots; IAHC marks 40 years on Knox Ave; Chicago hosts the Midwest Fleadh (April).

FitzGerald's listed on the National Register of Historic Places; Old Town School serves 33,845 students and its Square Roots festival draws a record 45,000+; Two Way Street adds Nordic jams and dances; Davenport's ends its cabaret format.

Celtic Knot reopens; McNally's St. Charles session starts; Bluegrass Breakdown at Judson & Moore begins; Hailstorm bluegrass jam goes weekly; Plank Road turns 40; Two Way Street launches the Nordic Jam and Nordic Dance (Oct).
Juan Díes and Victor G. Pichardo of Sones de México named NEA Fellows; 73rd Chicago Powwow (Oct 3); Midwest SOARRING cancels its Harvest Pow Wow; the IPA announces its 2027 convention for Erie, PA.
66th UChicago Folk Festival (Feb); 40th Chicago Scots Highland Games (June); 50th Fox Valley Folk Festival (Sep 6-7).

66th University of Chicago Folk Festival (Feb); Midwest Sacred Harp Convention at the Broadway Armory (May); 41st Woodstock Folk Festival (July); 50th Fox Valley Folk Festival (Labor Day); Ted Johnson dies at 98 (Oct 10); Hey Nonny listed for sale (October).
Comhaltas North American Convention in Northbrook (April); Fiddle Club Dunelands chapter in Miller Beach, IN; new Galway Arms session line-up (Sept); Chicago Reader feature on Queer Contra (May).

character_notes.history_festivals: Chicago's folk history rests on three institutions: a 19th-century police chief's Irish tune-collecting network, a 1920s barn-dance radio show that the Grand Ole Opry copied, and the Old Town School of Folk Music (1957), now a 24,000-student community school. Its signature is documentation and institution-building more than any one style. The 'Chicago Reel', 'Chief O'Neill's Favourite' and 'Sergeant Early's Dream' are played worldwide because Chicago policemen wrote them down. The 1970s singer-songwriter club scene (the Earl of Old Town, 1962-1984) outlasted the national folk bust. The old-time scene plays Midwestern (Illinois/Indiana) repertoire rather than Appalachian, through the Volo Bogtrotters, Chirps Smith and Paul Tyler. Geographically, history and festivals split three ways: a North Side corridor (Old Town, Lincoln Park, Lincoln Square, Mayfair/IAHC, Evanston); the South Side Irish (Brighton Park, Bridgeport, Beverly, Gaelic Park in Oak Forest); and suburban festivals on the rim (Geneva, Wheaton, Frankfort, Berwyn, Libertyville). Festivals cluster in summer (Blues in June, Square Roots and Gospel in July, Gaelic Park in August, Fox Valley on Labor Day), but the oldest, UChicago, is a February tradition.

surprises: Chicago's police chief compiled the 'bible' of Irish dance music. Francis O'Neill (chief 1901-05) put traditional musicians on the force, and the reel 'Sergeant Early's Dream' is named for a Chicago cop. 'The Chicago Reel' itself is older: it appears in an 1883 Leitrim manuscript and only got the Chicago name in O'Neill's 1907 book.

Session density is extraordinary: about 89 Irish sessions a month. One pub, the Galway Arms, runs four free sessions a week, and one accordionist, Jimmy Keane, leads or co-leads five regular sessions.

The Grand Ole Opry copied Chicago. George D. Hay announced WLS's National Barn Dance (1924) before going to Nashville, and its first house-band leader, Tommy Dandurand, was a retired Kankakee streetcar operator.

The Old Town School of Folk Music began as $2 guitar lessons in a living room in Oak Park. It is now a $17.6M-a-year school with 33,845 students, and toddlers (Wiggleworms) out-register string-band students about 3 to 1. It nearly died in 1981, when teachers worked without pay.

Chicago's busiest contra dance is held weekly in the 4th-floor ballroom of the Irish American Heritage Center, the same building as a weekly Irish session, the Friday céilís and the Comhaltas branch. Even so, modern western square dance clubs still schedule about six dances for every contra.
Old-time is the weak spot: the only weekly open old-time jam is in a pizza parlour (Borelli's 'Banjo After Dark'), and no fiddle contest runs inside a metro of 9.4 million.

Liz Carroll, All-Ireland senior fiddle champion at 18 (1975) and NEA Heritage Fellow, never played music full-time; she worked as a professional nurse. The piper Joe Shannon was a Chicago firefighter, and NEA Fellow Milan Opacich built tamburitzas in the basement of a Gary firehouse.
The Fox Valley Folklore Society has held a weekly Wednesday sing-around since 1975, now in a brewpub in Aurora, and two monthly sea-shanty sings run a thousand miles from salt water.

Ted Johnson was at the Old Town School's opening night in 1957, co-founded the Chicago Sacred Harp Singers, wrote 'New Agatite' for the 1991 Sacred Harp, and was still taking Irish fiddle classes in his 90s. He died on Oct 10, 2026, at 98.

Polka is fading while górale (Polish Highlander) music is thriving in the same community. The national polka convention was invented in Chicago (1963) and leaves for Erie, PA in 2027, while Dom Podhalan's calendar fills with górale events.
Alan Lomax's October 1938 Chicago recordings include a Finnish woman, Mrs. Hulan, singing with a kantele.
Michael Flatley became an NEA Heritage Fellow in 1988, six years before Riverdance.
curiosities: Is the Old Town School (33,845 students, $17.6M) the largest community folk-music school in the US, and does any other metro have a single folk institution this dominant (Swallow Hill, Passim, Dusty Strings)?
Irish sessions per Irish-American resident: how do Chicago's ~89 a month compare with Boston, New York and Philadelphia, and are Chicago sessions unusually professional-led or pub-paid?
With ~89 Irish sessions but one weekly open old-time jam, does Chicago's old-time energy go into its contra bands instead? How does the ratio compare with Seattle, Portland and the Triangle?
Why does no old-time fiddle contest run inside the Chicago metro? Which top-20 metros host contests, and does contest culture track Southern migration?
Did WLS's National Barn Dance leave a lasting square-dance or barn-dance culture, and how does it compare with WSM/Nashville's influence on Southern metros?
Why did Chicago's singer-songwriter club scene (the Earl of Old Town, 1962-84) outlast the post-1965 folk bust when New York's and Boston's shrank?
Shape-note density: Chicago has about 6.4 local Sacred Harp singings a month for 9.4M people. How does singings-per-million compare with Boston, Minneapolis, Seattle and Atlanta?
Bomba schools, son jarocho fandangos and mariachi programs: how do Chicago's numbers compare with New York, Orlando, Los Angeles and Houston?
Is the AIC's Chicago Powwow (73rd year) the longest-running urban powwow in the US?
Do other metros have an ethnic heritage centre (like Chicago's IAHC) hosting a weekly contra dance, and what does that do for cross-tradition traffic?
Weekly song circles 40-50 years old (Fox Valley since 1975, Plank Road since 1985): which metros have sing-arounds this old, and is the church-basement coffeehouse a Midwestern pattern?
Is Midwestern (Illinois/Indiana) old-time repertoire preferred over Appalachian at Chicago jams, and does the same regional preference appear in Minneapolis and Detroit?
Modern western square dance still outnumbers contra about 6:1 in Chicago. Is MWSD shrinking faster here than in Sun Belt retiree metros?
Why did the largest Midwestern Irish festival grow 90 miles away in Milwaukee rather than in Chicago?
data_quality_notes:
MERGE NOTES (session coordinator): four parallel research threads (trad_dance, song_listening, heritage, history_festivals) were merged by name; per-row _threads shows the source thread. Headline per-month totals exclude rows that are outside the MSA, rows without 2024-2026 evidence (e.g. AIC drum & dance, last evidence 2023; Ravenswood Morris, no date found) and two aggregate rows reported separately in headline_stats.aggregates_not_in_totals: the Old Town School 'Second Half' singalongs (~60.6/month across 14 weekly slots; these are free public singalongs attached to classes) and the ~17 MCASD modern western square dance clubs (~35-49 dances/month, using 42). Including both aggregates, the total is about 352 events a month. Old Town School student figures: 33,845 total in 2025 = 24,542 in group classes + 5,060 private + 4,243 workshops (sources agree once split). NEA years for some Fellows were stated 'from memory' by a thread; Liz Carroll's arts.gov bio was spot-checked and confirms the nurse detail. Per-thread notes follow.

[heritage] Research ran under a heavily contended web_search rate limit, so most verification came from directly fetching organization pages. Facebook and Instagram, where many heritage groups post schedules, were not accessible; several vitality calls (son jarocho, Bosnian, Assyrian, Greek, Filipino, banda/norteño) rest on thin or aggregator evidence and are marked medium or low. The Encyclopedia of Chicago (encyclopedia.chicagohistory.org) was unreachable. When fetched by script, the IAHC's own domain (irish-american.org, and irishfestchicago.com) returned only a generic templated 'Irish American Heritage Archive' shell, so IAHC facts come from Wikipedia, Eventbrite listings and a 2026 secondary article. The AIC Drum & Dance page is dated 2023, so it is marked low. Blues jam lists from the Chicago Blues Guide (c. 2022) and Low-reen's list (2023) were used only as leads; only jams with 2025-26 listings were recorded. Festival founding years marked 'inferred' come from edition numbers, and organizers' own numbering is sometimes inconsistent (Fiesta del Sol 54th vs. 55th; Puerto Rican Fest '45th' vs. a parade '47th' vs. a 1966 first parade). Attendance figures were rarely available. The NEA list was pulled by state filter (IL, IN). Fellows who lived in Chicago but were listed under other states may be missing; a full-text scan of all 502 bios was not done. Geography: Kenosha County, WI is no longer in the MSA (2023 delineation); La Porte County, IN (Pinetop Perkins) and Urbana (Judith McCulloh) are outside and flagged. Not found: Czech, Norwegian, Arab (non-Assyrian), Ethiopian or Filipino rondalla ensembles with current activity.

[history_festivals] Research was slowed by a shared web_search rate limit, and tunearch.org and slippery-hill.com blocked automated access, so no TTA annotations or Slippery Hill Illinois listings were read directly. Chicago tune data comes from The Session's API and pages, irishtune.info and DrDosido instead; the 1001 tune number for 'The Chicago Reel' and its 1883 Leitrim source come only from search summaries citing TTA. The Encyclopedia of Chicago site was down. surprises_all_threads: Seventeen NEA National Heritage Fellows are listed as Illinois residents (sixteen in the Chicago metro) and one more in Schererville, IN, across blues, gospel, Irish, polka, tamburitza, Romanian cimbalom, tap, children's song and Mexican son. The newest are Sones de México's founders (2026).

Michael Flatley became an NEA Heritage Fellow in 1988, six years before Riverdance. Chicago tap Fellow Bril Barrett later toured with Riverdance, a Chicago loop between Irish step dance and Black rhythm tap.
NEA Fellow Milan Opacich, America's leading tamburitza maker, built his instruments in the basement of a Gary firehouse during slow shifts.
Polish Highlander ensemble Siumni has traveled every year since 2003 to a sheep 'redyk' in Idaho, where górale shepherds work.

The national polka convention was invented in Chicago (moonlight dances from 1960, first convention 1963), but the IPA's 2027 Festival & Convention moves to Erie, PA. Meanwhile górale music, from a newer wave of Podhale immigrants, fills Dom Podhalan's calendar.
Chicago's bomba scene supports two full-curriculum schools; every La Escuelita class for the coming semester was sold out in Oct 2026.
AIC's Chicago Powwow is in its 73rd year, and the center's own page says 'competition does not define the powwow': specials, not prize money.
Chicago's main blues jam is a ticketed show: $16.99 for Jimmy Burns' Wednesday jam at Buddy Guy's Legends. The University of Chicago's monthly jam is free.
The Cambodian heritage museum teaches pinpeat ensemble music as 'healing arts' for genocide survivors' families.
Folk forms double as protest tools across communities: son jarocho jaranas at marches (Jarochicanos), plena as protest song (SRBCC), pungmul in immigrant-rights organizing (HANA Center).
The Lithuanian ensemble Grandis and the American Indian Center were both founded in 1953, and both still meet weekly.
The Maxwell Street Klezmer Band invented its own line dance, the 'Matzorena'.

Chicago's police chief compiled the 'bible' of Irish dance music. Francis O'Neill (chief 1901-05) hired traditional musicians onto the force (James O'Neill, James Early, John McFadden, Barney Delaney), and the reel 'Sergeant Early's Dream' is named for a Chicago cop.

O'Neill once wrote a Chicago officer asking him to get the Havana police to 'dig up' his brother-in-law, the piper Barney Delaney, who had gone missing in Cuba. The description included 'mustache usually dyed'.
'The Chicago Reel' is not from Chicago: the tune appears in an 1883 Leitrim manuscript and only picked up the Chicago name in O'Neill's 1907 book.

The Grand Ole Opry copied Chicago. George D. Hay announced WLS's National Barn Dance for about 18 months before going to Nashville, and the Barn Dance charged admission, reportedly the only radio show that did.
Newspapers named the first Barn Dance fiddler (1924) as 'Timothy Cornrow from Ioway'; the house band leader who followed, Tommy Dandurand, was a retired Kankakee streetcar operator.
Among Alan Lomax's Chicago recordings from October 1938 is a Finnish woman, Mrs. Hulan, singing with a kantele, not blues or Irish music.

The Old Town School began as $2 guitar lessons in Dawn Greening's Oak Park living room. On opening night Frank Hamilton wrote Big Bill Broonzy's fingerpicking out in tablature on a blackboard and taught it to the crowd.
Today the Old Town School occupies a 1931 Art Deco public library; its baby-music program (Wiggleworms, 23% of 2016 enrollment) helps pay for less popular programs.

Earl Pionke opened the Earl of Old Town in 1962 and kept booking folk acts after the Gate of Horn closed and the boom faded, because he 'couldn't imagine Wells Street without folk music'. It lasted until 1984. The after-hours club behind it later became John Belushi and Dan Aykroyd's 'Blues Brothers' bar.

Joe Shannon (NEA Heritage Fellow) learned what Irish players call 'American-style' piping from 78s by Patsy Touhey and Tom Ennis. As a child he stuffed books under his shirt to hold the pipes up, and he was a Chicago firefighter.
Chicago-born Liz Carroll won the senior All-Ireland fiddle title at 18 in 1975, only the second American to do so, and spent her career working as a nurse.
Hull House folk dance teacher Mary Wood Hinman later trained the modern-dance pioneer Doris Humphrey.
The free Frankfort Bluegrass Festival in Will County booked Korea's Country GongBang, which sings bluegrass in English and Korean.
Chicago Scots (1845) calls itself the oldest not-for-profit in Illinois; its Wheaton Highland Games claim North America's largest pipe band competition.

In 1977 the Library of Congress recorded an Alabama-born woman fiddler, Nancy Buckalew, at Johnny's Tavern in Cicero. She had bought a fiddle again in 1969 because her children wanted to learn, and was teaching her grandson.
WFMT recorded 305 hours of UChicago Folk Festival tapes (1961-1995). They sit in the Chicago Public Library, with 125 hours digitized.
Ella Jenkins, Chicago's 'first lady of children's music', died in 2024 at 100; her Multicultural Children's Songs is Smithsonian Folkways' most popular release.

The University of Chicago Folklore Society reportedly turned down a hungry young Bob Dylan for the 1961 festival's local-folksinger hootenanny (the deciding vote was Paul Levy's), and he slept in the cupboard of a student apartment on 53rd Street for a few days (UChicago News / UChicago Magazine).

Chicago's Sacred Harp revival came through the folk scene, not church choirs. The Chicago group started with a choir director, Phil Trier, who asked 'Do you want to sound like a group of backwoodsmen?' and got a spontaneous 'yes!'. Chicago and downstate singers met when folkies in the audience at a Libertyville School of Folk Music concert turned up holding Sacred Harp books (sacredharp.com, 2017).

Ted Johnson was at the Old Town School's opening night in 1957, became its second teacher, taught yodeling there in the late 1990s, co-founded the Chicago Sacred Harp Singers, composed 'New Agatite' for the 1991 Sacred Harp, and was still taking Irish fiddle classes at the school in his 90s. He died on Oct 10, 2026 at 98.

The Old Town School is a $17.6M-a-year institution (2025) with 33,845 students and 276 teaching artists, yet its oldest tradition is a free, half-hour public singalong (the 'Second Half'), still offered in 14 weekly slots.
Old Town School class prices rose from $48 per 8-week session in the mid-1970s to $264 today, about 5.5 times, roughly in line with inflation.
Toddlers out-register fiddlers about 3 to 1: in 2025 Wiggleworms was 17.9% of the Old Town School's group-class registrations and 'String Band' 5.4%.
The Fox Valley Folklore Society has held a weekly Wednesday sing-around since 1975, more than 50 years, and today it meets in a brewpub, the Two Brothers Roundhouse in Aurora.

Two monthly sea-shanty sings run a thousand miles from salt water: Chicago Shanties at the Old Town School (282-member list) and the Fox Valley shanty sing at the Batavia Public Library. The Old Town School even offers a class on songs sailors sang 'around the great inland seas'.

Two Way Street Coffee House is a 60-seat church-basement room with a $10 suggested donation, yet it belongs to Local 1000 (the traveling musicians' union) and guarantees performers scale pay. Its 2020 livestreams set the record for donations to a single concert in its 50-year history.

FitzGerald's in Berwyn, credited with bringing zydeco and Clifton Chenier to Chicago audiences, is in a building that was a 1911 dance hall and, as Club Ritz, a hangout for Capone's gang. In 2025 it became the first music venue in Illinois on the National Register of Historic Places.

WFMT's Midnight Special, Chicago's longest-running radio program (1953), was started by Mike Nichols, who later directed The Graduate. Rich Warren co-hosted or hosted it for 37 years and never missed an episode.
During its 1990s boom the Old Town School seriously considered dropping the word 'folk' from its name more than once, and its 1998 move to a derelict Art Deco library helped gentrify Lincoln Square.
In 1981 the Old Town School was down to about 300 students a week and nearly $60,000 in the red. It survived partly because teachers agreed to work without pay.
Harmony's Chicago factory mass-produced about ten million guitars between 1945 and 1975, so plausibly more Americans learned folk songs on a Chicago-made first guitar than on one from anywhere else.

In the middle of the 2018-19 fight over selling its historic Armitage building, the school's part-time teaching artists unionized with the Illinois Federation of Teachers; the first contract took until June 2022.

Chicago's busiest contra dance is a weekly Monday dance in the 4th-floor ballroom of the Irish American Heritage Center. The same building hosts a Thursday Irish session, Friday céilís, the Comhaltas branch and the Thanksgiving contra weekend, so one Irish-American centre anchors American, Irish and English dance traditions.
A single pub, the Galway Arms in Lincoln Park, runs four free public trad sessions a week (Sun, Tue, Wed, Thu).

The Irish Musicians Association of America was founded in Chicago in 1956, at a hotel meeting with players from eight US cities. Its president calls it the oldest Comhaltas branch in the US, and Chicago hosted the Comhaltas North American Convention in April 2026.
Chicago's only weekly open old-time jam is in a pizza parlour (Borelli's, "Banjo After Dark"), and some weeks the opening act is a klezmer orchestra.
One accordionist, Jimmy Keane, leads or co-leads five regular sessions and keeps the city's de facto session list.
Queer Contra Chicago was among the first local dances to drop "ladies/gents". The CBDC now uses larks and robins by default, as a CBDC board member predicted in 2019.
Modern western square dancing still out-schedules contra about six to one: roughly 35-49 club dances a month from about 17 MCASD clubs, against about 7 contra dances.

Chicago morris goes back to 1910, when UChicago's high-school boys danced "Bean Setting", learned from an Oxfordshire bricklayer's family by Hull House teacher Mary Wood Hinman. Today Pullman Morris and Sword members dance up the May Day sun at Promontory Point at about 4:45am.
The Thursday Israeli folk dance in Evanston has met weekly since March 1974.
The trad map is spreading into the far exurbs: two McHenry County breweries and pubs started monthly sessions in 2024, both run by the same organiser.
The Fiddle Club of the World is a Chicago invention (2008), with a new 2026 "Dunelands Chapter" in a house in Miller Beach on the Indiana dunes.
Former Chicago Tribune columnist Eric Zorn calls contras and plays fiddle and guitar in a Monday-night dance band, the Ladies Banjo Society of Illinois.
